articles.label: ACCOUNTABILITY
articles.headline: Escambia County's $47M reserves question: Who decides when rainy day funds get spent?
articles.dek: County commissioners approved dipping into reserves three times this fiscal year with little public debate. A look at the policies—or lack thereof—governing when surplus dollars leave the vault.
brief: Escambia County commissioners have approved three separate reserve fund withdrawals totaling $8.2 million since October 2025
The county maintains approximately $47 million in general fund reserves but operates without a formal written policy dictating when or how those funds can be accessed
Financial oversight experts say the absence of codified guidelines creates risk for inconsistent decision-making and reduces public accountability
articles.body:
The agenda item appeared on page 47 of the consent calendar. No discussion. No questions from the dais. In under ten seconds on a Tuesday morning in March, Escambia County commissioners approved transferring $2.1 million from reserve funds to cover unexpected repairs at the main jail facility.

It was the third time this fiscal year the board had reached into the county's rainy day account. The first came in October—$3.4 million for emergency drainage work after flash flooding damaged infrastructure in Cantonment. The second arrived in January—$2.7 million to address a budget shortfall in the Sheriff's Office overtime account.

Combined, the withdrawals represent $8.2 million drawn from reserves in seven months. The money came out fast. The public debate about it never really happened.

The $47 Million Question

Escambia County maintains approximately $47 million in its general fund reserve account, according to the most recent financial statements filed with the state. That figure represents roughly 18 percent of the county's annual general fund budget—a healthy cushion by most municipal finance standards.

What the county does not maintain is a formal written policy governing when those reserves can be tapped, under what circumstances, with what approval thresholds, or how quickly the funds must be replenished.

"We follow best practices," County Administrator Wes Moreno said when asked about reserve fund guidelines during a budget workshop last month. "The board has full authority over fund balance decisions."

That authority is not in dispute. What remains unclear is how that authority gets exercised—and whether residents have any meaningful way to anticipate or scrutinize reserve spending decisions before they happen.

What Other Counties Do

A survey of Florida's 67 counties reveals significant variation in how reserve funds are governed. Some operate like Escambia—with informal practices and board discretion. Others have adopted detailed written policies.

Hillsborough County's reserve fund policy runs nine pages. It establishes minimum balance requirements, defines emergency conditions that justify withdrawals, requires supermajority votes for draws exceeding certain thresholds, and mandates replenishment plans within 36 months.

Orange County requires that any reserve withdrawal above $500,000 appear as a standalone agenda item—not buried in consent calendars—with a staff memo explaining the necessity and alternatives considered.

Neighboring Santa Rosa County adopted a formal reserve policy in 2019 following recommendations from its external auditor. The policy sets a floor of 15 percent of the general fund budget and requires public hearings before any withdrawal that would drop reserves below 20 percent.

Escambia County has no such policy on the books. When asked whether one was under consideration, County Attorney Alison Rogers said she was not aware of any pending ordinance or resolution addressing reserve fund governance.

Three Withdrawals, Three Different Processes

The three reserve fund withdrawals approved this fiscal year followed different paths to the commission chamber.

The October drainage emergency came to the board as a standalone item following a declared local state of emergency. County staff presented damage assessments and cost estimates. Three commissioners asked questions. The vote was unanimous.

The January Sheriff's Office transfer appeared in a budget amendment package alongside 14 other line-item adjustments. The reserve withdrawal was mentioned in the staff summary but not highlighted. No commissioner commented on it specifically. The package passed 4-1, with Commissioner Steven Barry voting no on unrelated grounds.

The March jail repair funding landed on the consent calendar—a batch of routine items approved collectively without individual discussion unless a commissioner or member of the public pulls an item for separate consideration. No one did.

"That's just how the process works," said Jeff Bergosh, the District 1 commissioner who chairs the board. "If someone has concerns, they can pull something from consent. That's what the mechanism is for."

The mechanism requires that someone notice the item first.

The Visibility Problem

Government finance experts say consent calendar placement of significant reserve withdrawals creates accountability gaps—even when technically permissible.

"Reserve funds are the public's savings account," said Rebecca James, a professor of public administration at the University of Central Florida who studies municipal finance practices. "When you're spending savings, that should be a visible decision. Burying it procedurally undermines public trust even if nothing improper occurred."

James pointed to research showing that consent calendar items receive dramatically less media coverage, public comment, and commissioner engagement than standalone agenda items—regardless of dollar amounts involved.

Escambia County's consent calendar regularly includes items ranging from routine contract renewals to multi-million-dollar expenditures. The March 18 meeting where the jail repair funding passed included 23 consent items totaling more than $11 million in combined spending.

The meeting's public comment period—held before the consent vote—drew four speakers. None mentioned reserve funds.

What the Numbers Show

County budget documents indicate Escambia's reserve balance has fluctuated significantly over the past decade. Following Hurricane Ivan in 2004 and the Deepwater Horizon oil spill settlement in 2016, reserves swelled with insurance and legal proceeds. Following the COVID-19 pandemic, federal relief funds provided additional cushion.

But underlying structural pressures remain. The county's general fund expenditures have grown an average of 4.2 percent annually over the past five years, while revenue growth has averaged 3.1 percent. The gap has been covered through a combination of one-time revenues, deferred maintenance, and occasional reserve draws.

The $8.2 million withdrawn this fiscal year represents approximately 17 percent of the reserve balance—a significant but not alarming reduction according to Government Finance Officers Association guidelines, which recommend maintaining reserves equal to at least two months of operating expenditures.

Escambia currently exceeds that threshold. The question is whether ad hoc withdrawals will continue, and whether the public will know about them until after the fact.

What Commissioners Say

Commissioner Barry, who represents District 4 and has served on the board since 2012, said he supports developing a formal reserve policy but has not made it a priority.

"Every year we have budget workshops, and every year we talk about fund balance," Barry said in an interview. "A written policy might be useful for consistency. But the board changes, priorities change. I'm not sure how much a policy actually constrains anything."

Commissioner Lumon May, who represents District 3, said he would support bringing a draft policy to the board for consideration. "Transparency is always good," May said. "If we're going to spend rainy day money, people should know why and how."

Neither commissioner indicated they would introduce a formal proposal. When asked who would need to initiate such a policy, both pointed to county administration.

Moreno, the county administrator, did not respond to a follow-up request for comment on whether his office would bring a draft reserve policy to the board.

Looking Ahead

The fiscal year 2027 budget process begins next month with initial department submissions due to the county's Office of Management and Budget by June 15. Commission budget workshops are scheduled for July.

Whether reserve fund governance will appear on that agenda remains unclear. No commissioner has requested it. No staff memo has suggested it. The $47 million will sit in the vault, available for the next emergency—or the next consent calendar vote—whichever comes first.

The Flightline has filed a public records request for all internal communications regarding reserve fund withdrawals over the past 18 months. Those documents were not available before publication. This story will be updated when records are received.

articles.label: Investigation
articles.headline: The Palafox Pier rebuild is two years behind schedule. What happened?
articles.dek: Promised for completion by summer 2024, the downtown pier project has blown past deadlines and budgets. Contractors blame permits. The city blames contractors. Fishermen just want somewhere to cast a line.
brief: The $4.2 million Palafox Pier reconstruction, originally scheduled for summer 2024 completion, remains unfinished with no firm end date
Project costs have ballooned to $6.8 million amid disputes between the city and contractor Coastal Marine Construction over permit delays and change orders
Downtown fishermen and tour operators say the prolonged closure has cost them thousands in lost income and driven regulars to other piers
articles.body:
The chain-link fence has been up so long it's rusting.

Three years ago, when Pensacola closed the Palafox Pier for a full reconstruction, city officials promised a summer 2024 reopening. A new fishing deck. ADA-compliant railings. LED lighting. A rebuilt T-head wide enough for wedding photos and Saturday morning anglers alike.

That summer came and went. So did the next one. Now, in May 2026, the pier remains a construction zone. Orange barrels. Plywood barriers. A single porta-john baking in the sun.

What happened?

The answer depends on who you ask.

The city's version

According to Pensacola Public Works Director Martina Solis, the project fell behind because of the contractor. Coastal Marine Construction, the Navarre-based firm awarded the $4.2 million contract in January 2023, missed key milestones within the first six months.

"They were behind on mobilization. Behind on pile driving. Behind on concrete pours," Solis said in an interview last week. "At a certain point, you're just playing catch-up."

The city issued formal notices of default in March 2024 and again in September 2024. Both times, Coastal Marine responded with cure plans that the city accepted. Both times, delays continued.

Solis declined to say whether the city is considering terminating the contract. "That's a legal question," she said. "I'm focused on getting the pier built."

The contractor's version

Coastal Marine owner Dale Hutchins sees it differently.

In a phone interview, Hutchins blamed the Florida Department of Environmental Protection for taking nine months to approve a modified permit for the new T-head configuration. The original design called for a 40-by-60-foot platform. Environmental reviews required a smaller footprint, which meant redesigning the structural supports.

"We had crews sitting idle," Hutchins said. "You can't drive piles into Pensacola Bay without DEP sign-off. The city knew that. They should've had the permits locked before they bid the job."

He also pointed to 14 change orders the city issued after construction began—modifications to lighting, railing height, and deck surfacing that added scope and cost.

"Every change order is a negotiation," Hutchins said. "That takes time."

Records obtained through a public records request show the 14 change orders totaled $1.3 million. The city approved each one.

The numbers

The original contract: $4.2 million.

Current project cost: $6.8 million.

Original completion date: July 2024.

Current projected completion: "Late 2026," according to the city's most recent update to the council.

That's a 62 percent cost increase and a timeline that's stretched past two years behind schedule.

City Council member Tenley Harper, who represents District 6 and chairs the budget committee, called the overruns "unacceptable" at an April 22 meeting.

"This was supposed to be a straightforward rebuild," Harper said. "We've now spent enough to build a new pier twice over, and we still don't have a pier."

She requested an independent audit of the project. City Administrator Keith Wilkins said the request was "under review."

Who pays

The original $4.2 million came from a combination of sources: $2.1 million from the Pensacola general fund, $1.5 million from a Florida Boating Improvement grant, and $600,000 from BP oil spill settlement funds.

The additional $2.6 million? All city money.

Solis said the city dipped into reserves and reallocated funds from other parks projects. The Bayview Community Center roof replacement, originally scheduled for 2025, has been pushed to 2027. So has resurfacing at Hitzman Park.

"We had to make choices," Solis said.

The fishermen

On a Tuesday morning, the sidewalk along Palafox Street ends at that rusting fence. Beyond it, the skeletal frame of the new pier juts into the bay. No decking. No railings. No fish.

Ronnie Baxter has fished the Palafox Pier since 1987. He's 71 now. Bad knees. He liked Palafox because it was flat, close to parking, and had a bench where he could sit between casts.

"I've been driving out to the Pensacola Beach pier," he said. "Costs me ten bucks in gas every time. And I got to stand the whole time."

He used to come three times a week. Now it's once, maybe twice a month.

"They said two years. Okay. Two years I can wait. But this?" He gestured at the fence. "This is something else."

Charter captain Luis Medina, who runs sunset cruises out of the downtown marina, said the pier closure has hurt his business too. He used to pick up walk-on passengers who were hanging around the pier. Now there's no foot traffic.

"People don't come downtown to look at a construction site," Medina said. He estimates he's lost $15,000 in bookings over the past two years.

What's next

At the April 22 council meeting, Solis presented a revised timeline. Pile driving, she said, was 85 percent complete. Decking would begin in June. Electrical and lighting by August. Final inspection by October or November.

"We're in the home stretch," she said.

Council member Harper wasn't convinced. "We've heard 'home stretch' before," she said. "I'll believe it when I see fishermen on that pier."

Hutchins, the contractor, was more cautious in his estimate. "Weather's a factor. Supply chain's a factor. I'd say end of the year is realistic. But I'm not making promises anymore."

Ronnie Baxter, the fisherman, has a simpler metric.

"When that fence comes down," he said, "I'll be first in line."

He pointed his truck toward Pensacola Beach.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: Blue Angels homecoming week brings 150,000 visitors—and a housing shortage nobody planned for
articles.dek: With the team's return from winter training overlapping with Memorial Day crowds, short-term rentals are maxed out and hotels are gouging. Local officials say they saw it coming but couldn't act in time.
brief: Blue Angels homecoming show expected to draw 150,000+ visitors May 22-24, overlapping with Memorial Day weekend for first time since 2019
Short-term rental inventory exhausted across Pensacola Beach and downtown; hotel rates averaging $489/night, up 340% from typical May pricing
Escambia County tourism officials acknowledged scheduling conflict in February but said coordination with Navy came too late to expand lodging capacity
articles.body:
The parking lot at the National Naval Aviation Museum was empty on a Tuesday morning last week. By Memorial Day weekend, it will hold 8,000 cars. The grass overflow fields will hold another 6,000. And somewhere beyond the fence line, six F/A-18 Super Hornets will scream through a cloudless May sky while 150,000 people crane their necks upward.

The Blue Angels are coming home.

They do this every year, returning from winter training in El Centro, California, to their home base at NAS Pensacola for the season's first hometown show. It is the biggest annual event in Escambia County. It is also, this year, a logistics disaster that local officials saw coming and couldn't stop.

The 2026 homecoming show falls on May 22-24. Memorial Day is May 25. For the first time since 2019, the two events overlap, creating a nine-day stretch that has overwhelmed the region's lodging capacity and left thousands of would-be visitors scrambling for places to sleep.

The numbers don't work

Escambia County has approximately 4,200 licensed short-term rental units. Pensacola Beach accounts for 2,800 of those. As of Monday morning, exactly 23 were available for any night between May 20 and May 26, according to a Flightline analysis of listings across Airbnb, Vrbo and local rental agencies.

Hotels aren't much better. The Hampton Inn on Pensacola Beach—typically $139 per night in May—is asking $579 for May 23. The Hilton downtown wants $612. The Days Inn on Pensacola Boulevard, a budget property that rarely breaks $80, has rooms listed at $289.

The average hotel rate across the Pensacola metro for homecoming weekend is $489 per night, according to data from STR, a hospitality analytics firm. That's up 340% from the typical May average of $111.

"I've been coming to this show for fifteen years," said Mark Dunaway, a retired Navy pilot from Atlanta who attended the 2024 homecoming. "I usually book in February and pay maybe two hundred a night. This year I tried to book in January and everything was already gone. Everything."

Dunaway said he's staying in Mobile and driving in each day. It's 60 miles each way.

A foreseeable collision

The scheduling conflict was not a surprise. Memorial Day falls on the last Monday of May every year. The Navy sets the Blue Angels' performance schedule 18 months in advance. Anyone with a calendar could see this coming.

Someone did. Nicole Stacey, president and CEO of Visit Pensacola, said her office flagged the overlap in February 2025, shortly after the Navy released the 2026 schedule.

"We raised it with the county, we raised it with the Navy, we raised it with our hotel partners," Stacey said in an interview Friday. "Everyone agreed it was a concern. But by that point, the schedule was set. The Navy had already coordinated with the FAA, with the Coast Guard, with all the agencies that have to sign off. Moving the show wasn't really an option."

The Navy's Blue Angels public affairs office did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, whose district includes Pensacola Beach, said the county discussed the scheduling issue at a closed-door workshop in early March. No action was taken.

"What were we going to do?" Bergosh said. "Build more hotels in three months? We don't control the private market. We don't control the Navy's schedule. We flagged it, we communicated it, and we hoped the market would adjust."

The market did adjust. It adjusted prices upward.

Who gets squeezed

The people most affected aren't the visitors willing to pay $500 a night. They're the ones who can't.

Teresa Mullins teaches fourth grade in Birmingham. She and her husband have brought their two sons to the homecoming show six of the last eight years. They stay at the same beach condo every time, a two-bedroom unit that rents for $175 a night.

This year the owner wanted $650. Per night. For four nights minimum.

"That's our whole summer vacation budget," Mullins said by phone. "We're not rich people. We just wanted to take our kids to see the Blue Angels. Now we're not going."

She's not alone. A Facebook group called "Blue Angels Fans" has more than 40,000 members. In the last three weeks, the group has been flooded with posts from families canceling trips, asking about day-trip options from as far as New Orleans, and venting about prices they call "criminal."

One member posted a screenshot of a Perdido Key condo listing: $1,200 per night, four-night minimum, $400 cleaning fee. The unit typically rents for $180.

"This is price gouging, plain and simple," the post read. It had 847 reactions.

What price gouging actually means

Florida's price gouging statute, codified in Florida Statute 501.160, prohibits charging "unconscionable prices" for essential commodities during a declared state of emergency. Hotel rooms are specifically listed as a covered commodity.

There is no state of emergency for the Blue Angels homecoming show.

"That's the key distinction," said David Clements, a consumer protection attorney in Tallahassee who has litigated price gouging cases. "Outside of an emergency declaration, there's no cap on what a hotel or rental owner can charge. It might feel unfair. It might be unfair. But it's not illegal."

Clements said the only remedy for consumers is to not pay.

"Vote with your wallet," he said. "If nobody books at those prices, the prices come down. But if people pay, well, that's the market telling you what a room is worth that week."

Some people are paying. The Margaritaville Beach Hotel on Pensacola Beach told The Flightline it is fully booked for homecoming weekend at an average rate of $549 per night. A front desk employee, who asked not to be named because she wasn't authorized to speak publicly, said rooms sold out in February.

"We could have charged more," she said. "Looking at what everyone else is asking, we probably left money on the table."

The capacity question

Pensacola's lodging shortage isn't new. It's a chronic condition that flares up during peak events. The Foo Fighters concert at the Pensacola Bay Center in 2023 strained hotel capacity. The Ironman triathlon does it every November. The Blue Angels show does it every May.

What's different this year is scale. The overlap with Memorial Day has essentially doubled demand during a period when supply was already insufficient.

Escambia County has added approximately 1,100 hotel rooms since 2019, mostly through the opening of the Embassy Suites downtown and the expansion of several beach properties. But the county has also added roughly 800 short-term rental licenses in the same period, suggesting that new construction has barely kept pace with demand growth.

"We need more rooms," said Stacey, the Visit Pensacola CEO. "That's been true for years. It's just more visible right now."

The county's 2024 tourism master plan called for 2,000 new hotel rooms by 2030. As of May 2026, only 340 have been permitted, and none are under construction.

"Development is slow," said Robert Mitchell, a commercial real estate broker who specializes in hospitality properties along the Gulf Coast. "Land is expensive. Construction costs are up 40% since 2020. Interest rates make financing harder. Developers look at Pensacola and they see the demand, but they also see the math. And the math doesn't always work."

What happens next

The Blue Angels will fly. They always do. The weather forecast for May 22-24 shows clear skies, light winds, temperatures in the mid-80s. Perfect conditions.

The crowds will come. Estimates from Visit Pensacola suggest 150,000 to 175,000 attendees over the three-day show, with another 50,000 to 75,000 visitors in town for Memorial Day activities unrelated to the air show.

Where all those people will sleep remains unclear.

Some will drive in from Mobile, from Panama City, from Destin. Some will camp at Big Lagoon State Park, where reservations sold out in January. Some will crash with friends, squeeze into overpriced rooms, or turn around and go home.

Commissioner Bergosh said the county will conduct an after-action review in June to assess what went wrong and how to prevent it.

"This won't happen again," he said. "We'll be more proactive about coordinating with the Navy on scheduling. We'll push harder on hotel development. We learned some lessons."

Teresa Mullins, the Birmingham teacher, won't be there to see if those lessons stick.

"Maybe next year," she said. "If we can afford it."
